newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich supporter says he should step aside.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich supporter says he should step aside.

text.p: Republican backing for the re-election of Newt Gingrich as House speaker cracked on Monday when one of his strongest supporters said he should step aside because of his ethics problems.

"One way we can put this behind us is to ask ... Speaker Gingrich to really exercise the ultimate profiles in courage by stepping aside, not standing for re-election as speaker, and allow somebody else to provide dynamic leadership," Representative Michael Forbes, Republican of New York, said.

His comment was significant since Forbes was one of the 74 Republicans swept into office two years ago on the revolutionary tide led by Gingrich and has been one of the speaker's strongest backers since.
Forbes spoke on MSNBC television as other Republicans in the House of Representatives continued to present a united front for Gingrich's re-election when the new Congress convenes on January 7.
"We have seen no erosion whatsoever," Republican Whip Tom DeLay said in a television interview on Sunday.

Gingrich admitted to a House ethics panel nine days ago that he had violated House ethics rules, providing inaccurate information and failing to ensure that a college course he taught complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt organisations for partisan political purposes.
Gingrich's admission was similar to a guilty plea to an indictment, avoiding the need for a "trial" by the ethics committee.

But the committee still has to decide on the punishment to be meted out and whether to hold public hearings in which details of the two-year investigation could be laid out and Gingrich could give his side.

The committee is under pressure to act before January 7. Because the 10-member committee is equally divided between the parties, Republicans need at least one Democrat to vote with them to secure majority approval for any action it takes.
Gingrich confidant Representative John Linder, Republican of Georgia, has called for public hearings this week.

But the committee's senior Democrat, Representative Jim McDermott of Washington, said in an interview reported by the Washington Post on Monday that because of the voluminous evidence involved he did not see how the procedure could be completed so quickly.

The committee could impose punishments ranging from a rebuke to expulsion. Republicans say that Gingrich's offences merit only a rebuke that would not jeopardise his bid to become the first Republican speaker to be re-elected in 68 years.
